mainEntity.name: What is an inner class in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: An inner class in Java is a class defined within the body of another class. Java has four kinds: (1) Member inner class — non-static class inside another class, has full access to enclosing instance members. (2) Static nested class — static class inside another class, no access to enclosing instance. (3) Local inner class — class defined inside a method or block, visible only within that scope. (4) Anonymous inner class — nameless one-time-use class that simultaneously declares and instantiates, commonly used to implement interfaces or extend classes on the fly. Inner classes enable logical grouping, encapsulation of helper types, and tighter coupling where appropriate.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a static nested class and an inner class?

acceptedAnswer.text: A static nested class is declared with the static keyword inside another class. It does NOT have access to the enclosing class's instance members — it can only access static members of the enclosing class. It can be instantiated without an instance of the enclosing class: new Outer.StaticNested(). A member inner class (non-static) has implicit access to all members (including private) of the enclosing instance. It REQUIRES an enclosing instance to be created: outer.new Inner(). The key test: does the nested class logically need to operate on the enclosing object's state? Yes → member inner class. No → static nested class.

mainEntity.name: Can an inner class access private members of the outer class?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — a member inner class (non-static) can access ALL members of its enclosing class, including private fields and private methods, directly by name. This is one of the primary benefits of inner classes — they can act as trusted helpers that have intimate access to the outer class's internals without exposing those internals to the rest of the codebase. A static nested class, however, can only access static members of the enclosing class — it has no access to instance members because it has no enclosing instance reference.

mainEntity.name: What is an anonymous inner class in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: An anonymous inner class is a class that is declared and instantiated in a single expression, with no class name. It simultaneously defines the class body and creates an instance. It must either extend a class or implement an interface. Syntax: new InterfaceOrClass() { // overridden methods here }. Anonymous inner classes were commonly used before Java 8 to implement single-method interfaces (Runnable, Comparator, ActionListener). Since Java 8, lambda expressions replace most anonymous inner class usage for functional interfaces — but anonymous classes are still needed when implementing interfaces with multiple methods or when local state is required.

mainEntity.name: Can we declare static members inside an inner class?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prior to Java 16, a non-static inner class (member inner class, local inner class) could NOT declare static members (except static final compile-time constants). This was because non-static inner classes are tied to an enclosing instance, and static members exist at the class level — the combination was considered semantically inconsistent. From Java 16 onwards (JEP 395, part of records and inner class improvements), inner classes CAN declare static members. Static nested classes have always been able to declare static members. Anonymous inner classes still cannot declare static members in most practical contexts.

sections.title: What is an Inner Class in Java?

blocks.text: A nested class (or inner class) in Java is a class defined inside the body of another class. The outer class is called the enclosing class. Java supports nesting classes for a fundamental reason: sometimes a class only makes sense in the context of another class, and co-locating them expresses that tight relationship clearly in the source code.

Consider a LinkedList class — it naturally has a Node concept. A Node only exists to serve the LinkedList; exposing it as a top-level public class would pollute the package's public API. Defining it as a static nested class inside LinkedList keeps it encapsulated. Similarly, event handlers, iterators, and builder objects often exist purely to serve one enclosing class — inner classes are the right tool.

Java's nested class mechanism is more powerful than simple co-location. A non-static inner class carries an implicit reference to its enclosing instance and can access all of the enclosing class's members — even private ones — without any getter methods. This is a deeper coupling than inheritance and is intentionally designed for tightly related types.

blocks.title: 🔑 Four Types of Nested Classes in Java
blocks.text: Java has exactly four kinds of nested classes: (1) Member Inner Class — non-static class inside an outer class body; has access to all enclosing instance members. (2) Static Nested Class — declared with 'static'; no enclosing instance; can only access outer static members. (3) Local Inner Class — class defined inside a method or block; visible only within that scope; can access effectively final local variables. (4) Anonymous Inner Class — nameless class declared and instantiated simultaneously; implements an interface or extends a class on the fly. Each serves a distinct design purpose.
Before diving into each type, here is a side-by-side overview to understand the key distinctions at a glance.

rows: Helper tightly coupled to outer instance state
Logically grouped helper with no outer-instance dependency
One-shot logic inside a method, multi-method interface

blocks.text: A member inner class is a non-static class declared directly inside another class's body — at the same level as instance fields and methods. It has an implicit reference to an instance of its enclosing class and can access all of the enclosing instance's members — private fields, private methods, everything — directly by name. Because of this implicit reference, creating a member inner class object requires an existing outer class object.

items.title: Instantiation Syntax
Key Characteristics
items.text:
1. Accesses all outer class members (even private) directly.
2. Holds implicit reference to enclosing instance (causes memory concern if outer is large).
3. Can be declared private, protected, public, or package-private.
4. Cannot declare static members (pre-Java 16).
5. Compiled to Outer$Inner.class with a synthetic field for the outer reference.

items.title: Best Use Case
items.text: Use when the inner class logically belongs to a specific instance of the outer class and needs to read/modify the outer instance's private state. Classic example: Iterator implementation inside a collection class — the iterator must navigate the collection's private internal structure (array, linked list nodes).

blocks.label: MemberInnerClass.java
lines: // AccountSummary needs intimate access to BankAccount's private fields
// It makes no sense to exist independently of a BankAccount instance
// ✅ Direct access to outer class private fields — no getters needed
return balance < 0;   // Direct access to outer 'balance'
// ✅ Must use outer instance to create inner class object

blocks.text: A static nested class is declared with the static keyword inside another class. It does not hold any reference to an enclosing instance. Consequently, it can only directly access static members of the outer class — it has no pathway to the outer class's instance fields or methods. It is instantiated without needing an outer class object: new Outer.StaticNested().

Despite the name, a static nested class is not limited in any other way — it can have instance fields, instance methods, its own constructors, and implement interfaces. The static in its declaration means only that it has no enclosing instance dependency, making it behaviorally similar to a top-level class that happens to live inside another class for namespace/packaging reasons.

blocks.label: StaticNestedClass.java
lines: // ─── Static Nested Class — Builder for HttpClient ─────────────────────
// Builder does NOT need access to any HttpClient instance
// It only builds configuration — static nested is the right choice
private String userAgent = DEFAULT_USER_AGENT; // ✅ outer static member OK
// Private constructor — forces use of Builder
public static int getRequestCount() { return requestCount; }
// ✅ No outer instance needed — new HttpClient.Builder()

blocks.title: 💡 Static Nested Class = Builder Pattern's Natural Home
blocks.text: The Builder pattern (as used by StringBuilder, Lombok @Builder, Protobuf, etc.) almost universally uses a static nested class for the Builder. The reason: a Builder logically belongs to the class it builds (Outer.Builder is self-documenting), but the Builder itself doesn't need any existing Outer instance — it creates one. A static nested class perfectly captures this relationship: grouped with the class it builds, but independent of any instance. This is why 'Outer.Builder' is idiomatic Java for the Builder pattern.

A local inner class is a class declared inside a method, constructor, or initializer block. Its scope is limited to the block in which it is declared — it cannot be instantiated or referenced from outside that block. Local inner classes can access: all members of the enclosing instance, and effectively final local variables of the enclosing method (variables that are assigned exactly once and never changed after that).

blocks.label: LocalInnerClass.java
lines: public void generateSalesReport(List<Double> monthlySales, String currency) {
// Declared inside this method — useful only within this method's logic
// Needs to format multiple things consistently throughout this method
// ✅ Access outer instance fields: companyName, reportTitle
// ✅ Access effectively final local var: currency
// 'currency' is effectively final — assigned once, never changed
// ─── Use the local class within the same method ────────────────────
if (sale > highest) { highest = sale; bestMonth = i + 1; }
// 'fmt' is only visible inside generateSalesReport() — perfectly scoped

blocks.title: 📌 Effectively Final — The Local Variable Access Rule
blocks.text: A local inner class (and anonymous inner class) can only access local variables from the enclosing method that are 'effectively final' — meaning they are assigned exactly once and never reassigned. Before Java 8, this required the explicit 'final' keyword. Since Java 8, the compiler infers effective finality — you don't write 'final', but if you try to modify the variable, the compiler errors: 'local variable X is accessed from an inner class; needs to be final or effectively final'. The reason: the inner class instance may outlive the method call (e.g., if passed out), so a snapshot of the variable is captured — a copy, not a reference to the stack slot.

An anonymous inner class is a class that is declared and instantiated in a single expression, with no class name. It must immediately extend a class or implement an interface. The class body follows the new ClassName() { ... } syntax. Anonymous classes were the primary mechanism for lightweight interface implementations in Java before lambda expressions arrived in Java 8.

// ─── Anonymous class vs Lambda for single-method interface ─────────

// Modern way — lambda (since Java 8) — same behaviour, 90% less code

sections.title: Anonymous Inner Class vs Lambda Expression

blocks.text: Java 8's lambda expressions replaced the most common use case of anonymous inner classes — implementing functional interfaces (interfaces with exactly one abstract method). However, anonymous classes are still necessary in scenarios where lambdas cannot be used. Understanding the distinction helps you choose the right tool.

Can declare its own instance fields
Cannot declare instance fields (stateless by design)
'this' refers to the anonymous class instance

Can extend an abstract or concrete class
Cannot extend a class — only implements functional interface
Lambda serialization is possible but complex

Handled via invokedynamic — lighter at class loading time
Multi-method interface, extending abstract class, need local state

sections.title: Access Rules — What Can See What

blocks.text: The access rules between inner classes and their enclosing classes are one of the most powerful (and potentially confusing) aspects of Java's nested class system. The rules differ significantly between member inner classes and static nested classes.

items.title: Member Inner Class → Outer Class
items.text: A member inner class can access ALL members of the enclosing class without restriction: public, protected, package-private, AND private fields and methods. It does so via its implicit reference to the enclosing instance. No getters needed. This is by design — the inner class is a trusted member of the outer class's implementation.

items.title: Static Nested Class → Outer Class
items.text: A static nested class can ONLY access STATIC members of the enclosing class directly. It has no enclosing instance, so instance members are inaccessible. To access instance members, it must receive an explicit outer class object reference (via constructor parameter or method parameter), just like any external class.

items.title: Outer Class → Inner Class
items.text: The outer class has FULL access to ALL members of its inner classes — including private members. This bi-directional access is a key design feature: inner classes can freely use private outer members, and the outer class can freely access private inner class members. This is the 'trusted helper' relationship.

items.title: Outside World → Inner Class
items.text: Access from outside depends on the inner class's access modifier: public inner class is accessible from anywhere (but still requires outer instance for non-static). private inner class is accessible only from within the outer class. protected follows normal protected rules. Package-private is accessible within the package. The outer class name is used to qualify: Outer.Inner or Outer.StaticNested.

blocks.label: AccessRules.java
lines: // ✅ Can access ALL outer members — including private
// ❌ Cannot access outer INSTANCE members — no enclosing instance
// ✅ Can access via explicit outer reference
System.out.println(inner.innerSecret); // ✅ 99 — outer can see inner private
// Static nested — no outer instance needed

blocks.text: Every instance of a member inner class holds a hidden reference to its enclosing class instance. This reference is how the inner class accesses the outer class's fields and methods. When there is no ambiguity, unqualified names like balance or deposit() automatically resolve to the enclosing instance's members. When there is ambiguity — for example, when the inner class has a field or method with the same name as the outer — you can use OuterClassName.this to explicitly refer to the enclosing instance.

blocks.label: EnclosingInstance.java
lines: // ─── Member inner class with same-named field ─────────────────────────
// Returns the OUTER instance — useful for chaining back
return EventBus.this; // ← reference to the enclosing EventBus
// Get back the outer instance from the inner class

blocks.title: ⚠️ Memory Leak Risk — Inner Class Holds Outer Reference
blocks.text: Every member inner class instance silently holds a reference to its enclosing outer class instance. This prevents the outer instance from being garbage collected as long as the inner instance is alive. If you create inner class objects and store them in long-lived collections (static maps, caches, event listener lists), the outer objects they reference will never be collected — a classic Java memory leak. Fix: if the inner class does not need outer instance access, make it static (static nested class). If you must use a non-static inner class in a long-lived context, manage its lifecycle carefully and remove references explicitly.

Shadowing in inner classes works across three levels: the inner class's own fields, the enclosing class's fields, and local variables in the enclosing method. When a name is used inside an inner class, Java resolves it in this order: inner class's own scope → enclosing instance's scope → enclosing method's local variables. OuterClass.this.fieldName explicitly reaches the enclosing instance when shadowing occurs.

blocks.label: InnerShadowing.java
lines: int value = 200;   // Inner field — shadows outer field
void demonstrate(int value) {  // Parameter — shadows inner field
int value = 50;   // local var — shadows outer field within this method
// Local inner class inside this method
// 'value' here — is local var (50) effectively final, captured

sections.title: Member Inner Class vs Static Nested Class — When to Use Which

blocks.text: The choice between a member inner class and a static nested class is one of the most important design decisions when nesting classes. The rule is simple but often forgotten: if the nested class does not need access to any instance member of the enclosing class, make it static. This preference is backed by Effective Java (Joshua Bloch, Item 24): "If you declare a member class that does not require access to an enclosing instance, always put the static modifier in its declaration."

items.title: Use Member Inner Class When…
items.text: 1. The nested class logically needs to READ or MODIFY the outer instance's private state. 2. Every instance of the nested class is fundamentally associated with one specific outer instance (e.g., an Iterator that navigates a specific collection's internal array). 3. The nested class is a helper type that is intrinsically bound to the outer class's lifecycle.

items.title: Use Static Nested Class When…
items.text: 1. The nested class does NOT need access to any instance member of the outer class. 2. The nesting is for logical grouping / namespace purposes only (e.g., Node inside LinkedList, Builder inside a domain class). 3. The nested class may need to be instantiated without an existing outer instance. 4. You want to avoid the memory leak risk of holding an outer reference.

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Member Inner Classes
items.text: Every member inner class instance carries a synthetic private field pointing to its enclosing instance (OuterClass.this). This means: (1) Every inner instance keeps the outer instance alive — memory leak risk. (2) Serialization becomes complex — the outer instance must also be serializable. (3) Slightly more memory per inner instance. (4) Cannot be used independently — always tied to an outer object. None of these apply to static nested classes.

blocks.text: These mistakes with inner classes are consistently found in Java code and often result in compile errors, memory leaks, or subtle runtime bugs.

blocks.label: InnerClassMistakes.java
lines: // ❌ MISTAKE 1: Trying to instantiate member inner class without outer instance
// ❌ COMPILE ERROR: no enclosing instance of type InnerClassMistakes
MemberInner m = outer.new MemberInner(); // ← correct syntax
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: Using non-effectively-final local var in inner class
// count++; // ❌ COMPILE ERROR: local variable count is accessed
//           // from an inner class; needs to be final or effectively final
System.out.println(count); // ✅ reading is OK if count is never changed
// count = 1; // This would break effective finality — compile error in run()
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Confusing 'this' in anonymous class vs lambda
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: Declaring static member inside non-static inner class (pre Java 16)
// static int counter = 0; // ❌ COMPILE ERROR before Java 16
static final int MAX = 100; // ✅ static final constant — always allowed
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: Forgetting static on nested class that doesn't need outer access
// BAD — holds unnecessary reference to InnerClassMistakes instance
int compute(int x) { return x * 2; } // Never touches outer fields!
// ✅ Fix: make it static — no outer reference needed

blocks.text: These inner class anti-patterns frequently surface in production code reviews and lead to memory issues, maintainability problems, or design violations.

items.title: Non-static Inner Class When Static Would Do
items.text: The single most common inner class anti-pattern — using a member inner class when the class never accesses any outer instance member. Every instance silently holds an outer reference, preventing GC. Effective Java (Item 24) is explicit: 'if a member class does not require access to an enclosing instance, always put static on it.' Treat static as the default and add non-static only when outer instance access is genuinely required.

items.title: Registering Inner Class Listeners Without Unregistering
items.text: Passing 'this' (a member inner class instance) to an event bus, listener registry, or observable — and never removing it — is one of the most common Java memory leaks. The registry holds a reference to the inner instance, which holds a reference to the outer, preventing GC of both. Always pair register() with unregister(), and use weak references (WeakReference<Listener>) in listener lists when object lifecycle is uncertain.

items.title: Anonymous Inner Classes for Multi-line Logic
items.text: Using an anonymous inner class with 20+ lines of logic makes the enclosing method illegible. If the anonymous class body is large, it deserves to be a named class — either a private static nested class, a separate package-private class, or a private method that returns the interface via a lambda. The rule: anonymous classes should be short and self-evident. If you need to write a comment inside one explaining what it does, extract it to a named class.

items.title: Deep Inner Class Nesting
items.text: Nesting inner classes more than two levels deep (class A { class B { class C {} } }) creates code that is almost impossible to read and reason about. Qualified names like A.B.C and reference patterns like A.B.this become incomprehensible. If you find yourself nesting three or more levels, redesign — flatten the hierarchy, use composition, or extract some classes to top-level or package-private classes.

items.title: Using Anonymous Class Instead of Lambda for Functional Interfaces
items.text: In Java 8+ code, writing 'new Comparator<String>() { @Override public int compare(String a, String b) { return a.compareTo(b); } }' instead of '(a, b) -> a.compareTo(b)' is verbose and dated. Lambdas are the modern replacement for anonymous classes implementing single-method interfaces. Code reviewers in 2026 will flag anonymous class usage for functional interfaces as a style violation. Always prefer lambdas (or method references) for functional interface implementations.

items.title: Public Non-static Inner Class in Library APIs
items.text: Exposing a public member inner class in a library's public API forces API consumers to handle the 'outer.new Inner()' instantiation syntax, which is unfamiliar and error-prone. Users also inherit the outer instance dependency implicitly. Library APIs should expose public static nested classes (or top-level classes) — never public non-static inner classes. If the inner class must be exposed publicly, a factory method on the outer class is a cleaner API: 'outer.createHelper()' returns the inner without exposing the syntax.

blocks.text: The following examples show idiomatic inner class usage found in real enterprise Java codebases — each demonstrating the appropriate type for its design scenario.

lines: // Node doesn't need to access the LinkedList instance — pure data holder
Node<T> newNode = new Node<>(item); // ✅ No outer instance needed for Node
// Iterator MUST access 'head' — the LinkedList instance's private field
// Non-static inner class is the correct choice here
private Node<T> current = head; // ✅ Accesses outer 'head' directly
return new ListIterator(); // Inner class — can only create from inside outer

// ─── Anonymous class — implements 2 methods (can't use lambda) ─

public boolean deliver(String recipient, String message) {
public void notify(String recipient, String message) {
// ✅ Static nested Config — no outer instance needed

sections.title: Java Inner Classes Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java mid-level and senior interviews, OCPJP certification exams, and design-focused technical rounds.

items.q: Q1. What are the four types of inner classes in Java? When would you use each?
items.a: Java has four types: (1) Member inner class — non-static class inside another class; use when the nested class needs access to the enclosing instance's private members (e.g., Iterator inside a collection). (2) Static nested class — static class inside another class; use for logical grouping when no outer instance access is needed (e.g., Node inside LinkedList, Builder pattern). (3) Local inner class — class inside a method; use for short-lived helpers that implement a multi-method interface and need local context. (4) Anonymous inner class — nameless, declared and instantiated simultaneously; use for one-time implementations of interfaces or abstract classes. Since Java 8, lambdas replace anonymous classes for functional interfaces.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between a static nested class and a member inner class?
items.a: Member inner class: declared without static, holds an implicit reference to the enclosing instance, can access ALL members (including private) of the enclosing instance directly, requires an outer instance to instantiate: outer.new Inner(). Static nested class: declared with static, has NO enclosing instance reference, can only access static members of the enclosing class directly, instantiated independently: new Outer.StaticNested(). Key design rule (Effective Java, Item 24): if the nested class does not need access to any instance member of the enclosing class, always declare it static. Non-static carries hidden memory and GC overhead.

items.q: Q3. Can an inner class access private members of its outer class? Give an example.
items.a: Yes — a member inner class has unrestricted access to all members of its enclosing class, including private fields and private methods, directly by name. This works because at the bytecode level, the Java compiler generates a synthetic accessor method in the outer class that the inner class calls. The access appears 'private' in source code terms but is bridged by the compiler. Example: a private BankAccount.balance field can be read and modified directly by BankAccount's AccountSummary inner class — balance appears as a simple name inside AccountSummary methods. This is by design — inner classes are trusted helpers of the outer class.

items.q: Q4. Why can't a local inner class access a non-final (or non-effectively-final) local variable?
items.a: A local inner class instance may outlive the method call that created it — for example, if the inner class instance is returned or stored in a field. If it could freely access a mutable local variable, that variable's stack frame might no longer exist when the inner class tries to use it (the method has already returned). Java's solution: when a local inner class (or anonymous class or lambda) accesses a local variable, it CAPTURES a COPY of that variable's value at the time of creation. For the captured copy to be reliable, the original must not change after capture — hence the 'effectively final' requirement. Compile error: 'local variable X is accessed from an inner class; needs to be final or effectively final'.

items.q: Q5. What is the difference between an anonymous inner class and a lambda expression?
items.a: Anonymous inner class: works with any interface (single or multiple abstract methods) and abstract classes; 'this' inside it refers to the anonymous class instance; can declare instance fields; creates a new class file at compile time. Lambda expression (Java 8+): only works with functional interfaces (exactly one abstract method); 'this' inside it refers to the ENCLOSING class instance (not the lambda); cannot declare instance fields; implemented via invokedynamic — no new class file. Practical rule: always prefer lambda for functional interfaces. Use anonymous class when: implementing multi-method interfaces, extending abstract classes, or needing instance-level state.

items.q: Q6. What is OuterClass.this and when is it needed?
items.a: OuterClass.this is the qualified form of 'this' used inside an inner class to explicitly refer to the enclosing class instance. It is needed when the inner class has a field or method with the same name as one in the outer class — creating ambiguity. Inside the inner class, an unqualified name 'balance' refers to the inner class's own field (if it has one). 'BankAccount.this.balance' unambiguously refers to the outer BankAccount instance's balance field. It is also used to return or pass the outer instance from within an inner class: 'return BankAccount.this;'.

items.q: Q7. How does a member inner class cause a memory leak?
items.a: Every instance of a member inner class holds a hidden (synthetic) reference to its enclosing outer class instance. As long as the inner class instance is alive (referenced by any object), the outer class instance CANNOT be garbage collected — even if no other reference to the outer exists. Memory leak scenario: an Android Activity creates an anonymous Runnable (or a non-static Handler subclass) and posts it to a long-running thread pool. The Runnable holds a reference to the Activity. Even after the Activity is destroyed, the thread pool keeps the Runnable alive, which keeps the entire Activity (and its view hierarchy, bitmaps, etc.) in memory. Fix: use static nested class + WeakReference to the outer if needed, or cancel/remove the inner class reference when the outer is destroyed.

items.q: Q8. Can we declare a static member inside a non-static inner class?
items.a: Before Java 16, no — a non-static inner class could not declare static members (except static final compile-time constants). The JLS prohibited this because a non-static inner class is tied to an enclosing instance, and static members exist at the class level — mixing them created semantic inconsistency. From Java 16 onwards (JEP 395, as part of records and sealed classes cleanup), inner classes CAN declare static members. Static nested classes have always supported static members. Anonymous inner classes and local inner classes still cannot declare static members in most practical scenarios.

items.q: Q9. What is the naming convention for compiled inner class files?
items.a: The Java compiler generates separate .class files for each inner class, following this naming convention: Outer$Inner.class for member inner class. Outer$StaticNested.class for static nested class. Outer$1.class, Outer$2.class, etc. for anonymous inner classes (numbered in source order). Outer$1MethodName.class or Outer$1.class for local inner classes (includes method context in some JVM implementations). The $ delimiter is the signal that a class file represents a nested type. You will see these files in your bin/ or target/classes directory. This is why class names with $ in reflection (e.g., getClass().getName()) indicate you are working with a nested class.

items.q: Q10. Why does Effective Java recommend preferring static nested classes over non-static inner classes?
items.a: Effective Java (Joshua Bloch, Item 24) gives three reasons to prefer static nested: (1) Memory: non-static inner class carries a hidden reference to the outer instance, preventing GC even when the outer object is no longer needed — a common source of memory leaks. (2) Serialization: if an inner class is serializable, the outer class must also be serializable (and serializable) — an unexpected coupling. (3) Clarity: a static nested class can be understood and instantiated independently — its relationship to the outer class is purely organizational. The rule: make a nested class non-static ONLY when you explicitly need it to access the enclosing instance. Otherwise, static should be the default.

items.a: Two problems: (1) Memory leak — the anonymous Runnable is a non-static inner class that holds an implicit reference to the MainActivity instance. The Thread holds the Runnable, the Runnable holds MainActivity. If the activity is destroyed while the thread is running, the GC cannot collect it. (2) Thread safety — rootView is accessed from a background thread, but UI views must only be touched on the main/UI thread. Fix: (a) Use a static nested class + WeakReference: private static class DataLoader implements Runnable { private final WeakReference<MainActivity> ref; DataLoader(MainActivity a) { ref = new WeakReference<>(a); } public void run() { MainActivity a = ref.get(); if (a != null && !a.isDestroyed()) a.runOnUiThread(() -> a.rootView.setVisibility(View.VISIBLE)); } } (b) Or use modern patterns: ViewModel + LiveData + Executor/Coroutine, which handle lifecycle automatically.

sections.title: Conclusion — Inner Classes: Precision Tools for Encapsulation and Cohesion

blocks.text: Java's four inner class types give you precision tools for expressing the exact degree of coupling between related types. Static nested classes are the workhorses of Java's standard library — Map.Entry, LinkedList.Node, and countless Builders are static nested classes. They provide logical grouping with zero coupling overhead. Member inner classes power Java's iterator pattern, giving iterators intimate, efficient access to collection internals without exposing that internals to the world. Anonymous classes remain the solution for multi-method one-off implementations even in the lambda era. Local inner classes are the rarest but occasionally perfect for method-scoped multi-method logic.

The single most impactful habit to develop: always default to static nested classes and only relax to non-static when you genuinely need outer instance access. This prevents memory leaks, simplifies serialization, and keeps instantiation straightforward. As Effective Java puts it — the static modifier is a signal of independence, and independence is almost always a virtue in software design.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Inner Classes

items.q: What is an inner class in Java?
items.a: An inner class (nested class) is a class defined inside another class. Java has four types: member inner class (non-static, has full access to enclosing instance), static nested class (no outer instance dependency), local inner class (defined inside a method, method-scoped), and anonymous inner class (nameless, declared and instantiated together). Inner classes enable tight encapsulation of helper types and allow related classes to be co-located without polluting the package's public API.

items.q: What is the difference between a static nested class and an inner class?
items.a: A member inner class (non-static) holds an implicit reference to the enclosing instance and can access all of its members including private. It requires an outer instance to instantiate: outer.new Inner(). A static nested class has no enclosing instance, can only access static outer members, and is instantiated independently: new Outer.Nested(). Effective Java recommends defaulting to static — use non-static only when outer instance access is genuinely needed.

items.q: Can an inner class access private members of the outer class?
items.a: Yes — a member inner class (non-static) can access ALL members of the enclosing class directly, including private fields and private methods. The compiler generates synthetic accessor bridges in the bytecode. A static nested class can only access static members of the outer class — it has no enclosing instance and therefore no access to instance-level private members without an explicit outer object reference.

items.q: What is an anonymous inner class in Java?
items.a: An anonymous inner class is declared and instantiated in a single expression with no class name: new InterfaceOrAbstractClass() { ... }. It implements/extends the specified type and is used once. Before Java 8, anonymous classes were the standard way to implement functional interfaces (Runnable, Comparator). Since Java 8, lambdas replace anonymous classes for single-method (functional) interfaces. Anonymous classes are still required for multi-method interfaces, extending abstract classes, or when local instance state is needed.

items.q: Can we declare static members inside an inner class?
items.a: Before Java 16, non-static inner classes could not declare static members (only static final compile-time constants were allowed). From Java 16 (JEP 395), inner classes can declare static members. Static nested classes have always been allowed to declare static members. Anonymous inner classes still cannot declare static members. This Java 16 change was part of aligning the semantics of records and other local class features.
